summary: Describes mechanisms to reduce the processing overhead of RSVP refresh messages, to remove the delay in recovering when a message is lost, and to keep reservation state without constantly retransmitting it.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP reservations need to be re-confirmed regularly, which is a lot of repeating. This cuts the repeating down and speeds up recovery.

questions: how to reduce rsvp refresh messages
what is an rsvp srefresh message
what is an rsvp bundle message
what is the rsvp message_id object
subtitle: Ways for RSVP routers to keep reservations alive and recover from lost messages without flooding each other with refreshes.

tldr.problem: Standard RSVP keeps state alive by resending full Path and Resv refresh messages for every session, which scales poorly, and a lost non-refresh message is only repaired at the next refresh interval.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds Bundle messages that pack many messages into one, MESSAGE_ID objects with acknowledgments and exponential back-off retransmission, and Srefresh messages that refresh state by listing message identifiers instead of resending whole messages.
tldr.outcome: Processing and bandwidth for refreshes drop, lost messages are repaired quickly, and nodes advertise support with a single header flag so nothing breaks with older neighbors. The RFC is a Standards Track document that has since been updated by RFC 5063.

today: RFC 2961 is a Proposed Standard, has not been obsoleted, and is updated by RFC 5063. The text itself says the exponential back-off procedures should be reviewed against operational experience before it advances to Draft Standard.

sections.title: The Refresh Problem in RSVP
sections.content:
Standard RSVP (RFC 2205) keeps its state alive with refresh messages. Each session needs Path and Resv messages sent every refresh period, so processing and memory costs grow with the number of sessions.

There is also a latency problem. If a non-refresh message is lost, RSVP only repairs it at the next refresh, so setting up or changing a reservation can take longer than some applications accept. Tuning the refresh period R does not fix both: a longer R cuts overhead but slows synchronization, and a shorter R helps recovery but raises the message rate. Tear messages (ResvTear, PathTear) are not retransmitted at all, so a lost tear leaves resources allocated until the cleanup timer expires.

The RFC separates trigger messages (they advertise new or changed state) from refresh messages (they repeat previously advertised state, and only Path and Resv can be refreshes). Its extensions address the volume and reliability problems without changing the refresh rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a teacher who has to ask every student "are you still here?" every few seconds. It wastes time, and if one answer gets lost nobody notices for a while. This RFC finds smarter ways to check in.

sections.title: The Refresh-Reduction-Capable Bit
sections.content:
A node announces support by setting a new flag, 0x01, in the Flags field of the common RSVP header. It means the node can receive the Bundle message, the MESSAGE_ID objects and Ack messages, and the MESSAGE_ID LIST objects and Srefresh message. The bit only matters between RSVP neighbors.

Nodes MUST watch the flag on every received message. If a neighbor's flag changes from capable to not capable, then, unless configured otherwise, Srefresh messages MUST NOT be used to refresh state toward it and Bundle messages MUST NOT be sent to it. A node that supports only reliable delivery (the MESSAGE_ID part) does not set the bit.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a little flag on every message that says "I understand the new tricks." If a neighbor stops waving the flag, you go back to the old way.

sections.title: Bundle Messages
sections.content:
A Bundle message has a header identical in layout to the RSVP common header, with message type 12, followed by one or more ordinary RSVP messages. A sub-message may be any type except another Bundle. The checksum may be zero because sub-messages carry their own checksums and INTEGRITY objects.

Bundling is optional, but a node MUST always be ready to receive standard messages. Bundles go hop by hop to a neighbor known to support them, as raw IP datagrams with protocol number 46. They SHOULD NOT carry the Router Alert option, each bundle occupies exactly one IP datagram, and the sender SHOULD limit how long a message waits to be bundled. Trigger messages should wait only a minimal time; refreshes may wait up to their refresh interval.

The receiver checks the version and checksum, then processes each sub-message as if it had arrived alone, apart from using the Send_TTL from the bundle header.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of mailing ten letters separately, you put them in one big envelope. The post office handles one envelope, and the neighbor opens it and reads each letter.

sections.title: MESSAGE_ID, Acknowledgments and Ack Messages
sections.content:
The MESSAGE_ID object (class 23) carries an 8-bit Flags field, a 24-bit Epoch and a 32-bit Message_Identifier. With the generator's IP address, it names one message on one hop. The Epoch is chosen randomly on restart and signals that the identifier sequence has reset. A refresh SHOULD reuse the identifier of the message that first advertised the state, while a trigger message MUST use a larger identifier than any used before with the same Epoch.

This lets a receiver tell a refresh from new state cheaply. A Path or Resv carrying the same identifier as the latest one for that state SHOULD be treated as a refresh, a larger one MUST be fully processed, and out-of-order messages SHOULD be silently dropped.

If the ACK_Desired flag (0x01) is set, the receiver SHOULD answer with a MESSAGE_ID_ACK object (class 24), which copies the Epoch and identifier. Acks ride in other RSVP messages or in a dedicated Ack message (type 13). Senders SHOULD retransmit unacknowledged messages faster than the refresh period, using the back-off procedure in the algorithms section. PathErr and ResvErr count as implicit acknowledgments.

For multicast, acknowledgments are spread over a random interval to avoid ACK implosion rather than suppressed. If the sender does not know how many next hops exist, it SHOULD expect a single response and let ordinary refreshes reach the rest.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message gets a number, like a tracking number on a package. The receiver can tell "I already saw this one" and can send back a "got it!" so the sender stops worrying.

sections.title: Summary Refresh (Srefresh)
sections.content:
The Srefresh message (type 15) refreshes state without resending Path or Resv messages. It lists the Message_Identifiers of the trigger messages that created the state, so only state first advertised with a MESSAGE_ID can be refreshed this way. Three list objects share class 25: MESSAGE_ID LIST (C_Type 1) for all Resv state and unicast Path state, and SRC_LIST and MCAST_LIST for multicast Path state, which add source (and for MCAST_LIST, group) addresses.

A receiver matches each identifier against installed state and treats a match as a normal refresh. If nothing matches, it returns a refresh NACK, which is a MESSAGE_ID_NACK object (C_Type 2), and the sender then MUST send the real Path or Resv message. For multicast an unmatched identifier is NACKed only if the node would forward data from that source to that group; otherwise it is ignored. NACKs also reveal route changes.

Srefresh must never let state time out, so its period MAY be shorter than the normal refresh period but MUST NOT be longer. A default generation interval of 30 seconds is suggested. When Srefresh refreshes a state, the standard refresh for it SHOULD be suppressed.

Because Srefresh cannot catch internal state corruption, the RFC recommends either storing a checksum such as MD5 over state to spot unsent triggers, or occasionally sending standard refreshes less often than the Srefresh interval.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of re-reading your whole homework to the teacher every day, you just say "same as assignment number 42." If the teacher has no assignment 42, they say so and you hand over the full page.

sections.title: Exponential Back-Off Retransmission
sections.content:
Messages sent with ACK_Desired are retransmitted by a rapid retransmission timer that starts small and grows exponentially. Implementations MUST use the described procedure or an equivalent. Three per-interface parameters control it: the initial interval Rf, the retry limit Rl (maximum transmissions without an ack) and the growth value Delta, where successive intervals differ by a factor of (1 + Delta).

Suggested defaults are Rf of 500 ms, Delta of 1 (doubling) and Rl of 3. The sender transmits, waits Rk seconds, multiplies Rk by (1 + Delta), and repeats until an ack arrives or the limit is reached. An ack received earlier cancels further retransmission.

The RFC notes that this back-off is a significant addition to RSVP and that experience, especially with multicast and ACK implosion, should be reviewed before advancing to Draft Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: If you call a friend and they do not pick up, you wait a little, try again, then wait twice as long, and so on, and you stop after a few tries.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
The extensions present no backward compatibility issues. A node that does not know the MESSAGE_ID class rejects it with an "Unknown Object Class" error because of its class number form, and the sender MUST then resend the message without the object. If it is not known whether a next hop supports Srefresh, standard Path and Resv refreshes MUST be used, and Srefresh SHOULD NOT be used when the routing next hop is not RSVP capable, unless an administrator has configured it for a network where all nodes are known to support it.

The Security Considerations section says only that no new security issues are raised and refers readers to RFC 2205.
sections.plainLanguage: If a neighbor does not understand the new tricks, you just go back to doing things the old way, so nobody gets confused.

fields.name: RSVP checksum
fields.desc: May be zero because sub-messages carry their own.

fields.name: Send_TTL
fields.desc: IP TTL used when sending, to detect non-RSVP hops.

fields.name: RSVP length
fields.desc: Total bytes of the bundle, header and sub-messages.

fields.name: Epoch
fields.desc: Changes only when the node or RSVP agent restarts.

fields.name: Message_Identifier
fields.desc: With the generator's IP address, identifies the message.
